turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on in, grab a seat. I'm Dr. Patel. What's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, it's my heel. First thing in the morning it just, it hurts.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Tell me what that feels like.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Like I'm stepping on a nail, right under the right heel. It's those first steps in the morning, and the same when I stand up from the register. Walk around a little and it eases. I don't know, doctor, it's strange.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the left one?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Left is okay, I think. I work the floor at the grocery, on my feet all shift, and I run a few evenings, about three miles.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the morning pain been with you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, the new shoes, I got these running shoes and they...
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shoes in a second, I promise.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Umm, two months. It's been two months.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it swell, or go numb, or shoot up the leg?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling, no numbness. It doesn't shoot anywhere.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything going on in the knees or the low back?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Just that one spot. I don't know.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking, if any?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, sertaline. Fifty milligrams, I think, every morning. For the anxiety. That's the only one.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bad reactions to a medicine, a rash, swelling, trouble breathing?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A few years ago I got all blotchy and itchy. Maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which, so I just...
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so that's fuzzy, and I'm not gonna pin a name on it. I won't be giving you an antibiotic or a pain pill for this anyway.

[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me read what they took out front. Pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse, uh, one oh two, no, hang on, I misread it, it's seventy-four. Temp is thirty-eight point three celsius.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last time in March you were sixty-eight, that was the pulse. Your last pressure was one-forty. You're a touch warm today. Feel sick at all on the way in?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know. I basically jogged from the bus. I don't feel sick, I don't think.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Shoes off for me. Show me the spot.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Here, bottom of the heel, kinda toward the inside. Those new ones are Nikes, the stiff kind, and I can't even remember when I bought them.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tender right on the plantar fascia where it grabs the heel bone. No puffiness. Achilles isn't sore when I squeeze it, and you point and flex just fine.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it broken? My cousin had a stress thing and she was in a boot for...

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to conclude it's a stress fracture, not with this story. What I'm settling on is plantar fasciitis. Heel fat pad irritation is the other possibility, less likely. The new shoes may be poking at it, but I won't call it a tear.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): So the shoes did it? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't say the shoes caused it. Err, hard heel cups don't help. No x-ray, no labs. What I want is calf stretches and a plantar stretch, morning and night, hold thirty seconds, 3 times each side.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty seconds, 3 times. Err, do I need one of those boots?

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): No boot. Pick up a soft heel cup or an over-the-counter insole with a little arch, for the work shoes and the running shoes. Ease the miles for a couple of weeks, but stay on your feet at the store, that's your job.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I've got this little 5k, I don't know if I can back off, but... yeah, I'll try the stretches.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks and we'll check those first steps. If it swells up or you can't put weight on it, call us before that, though I really don't expect it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Okay. Thanks, Dr. Patel.

spec.situation: Runner or shop worker with heel pain on the first steps in the morning for two months; new shoes mentioned; doctor suggests stretches and insoles; no tests.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Medication, dose, frequency, and indication stated; exact drug name uncertain as patient said 'sertaline' and 'I think'.
bad.text: sertaline (generic_name=sertraline, dose=50 mg, frequency=every morning, indication=anxiety, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Pain quality was described as 'like I'm stepping on a nail' under the right heel.
Left heel/foot was reported as okay (symptoms are unilateral on the right).
Patient reported not feeling sick despite the elevated temperature after doctor asked about this.
Doctor documented no x-ray and no labs were planned.
Doctor specifically said he was not concluding stress fracture and would not call it a tear.
Doctor said hard heel cups do not help.
